lessons.title: Cartesian form, conjugates and division
lessons.summary: Separate the two components, calculate in Cartesian form and use the conjugate to turn a complex denominator into a real one.
lessons.objective: Calculate with complex numbers in Cartesian form and explain simple Argand transformations.
lessons.before: Revise expanding two brackets, simplifying fractions and reading Cartesian coordinates.
lessons.method:
1. Read the signed real and imaginary coefficients.
  2. For a product, replace every occurrence of i squared by minus one.
  3. For division, conjugate the original non-zero denominator, then simplify both components.
mistakes: The imaginary part is a real coefficient.
Conjugation changes only the imaginary sign.
Conjugate the denominator rather than the numerator.
lessons.ideas:
Two complex numbers are equal when their real parts agree and their imaginary parts agree. On an Argand diagram \(a+b\mathrm i\) goes at \((a,b)\).

\((a+b\mathrm i)+(c+d\mathrm i)=(a+c)+(b+d)\mathrm i\). Subtract the two pairs component by component.

\((a+b\mathrm i)(c+d\mathrm i)=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)\mathrm i\). Work from the expansion when showing how you got the answer.

\(z^*=a-b\mathrm i\) and \(zz^*=a^2+b^2\). The product is strictly positive whenever \(z\ne0\).

Use \(\frac{c-d\mathrm i}{c-d\mathrm i}=1\) when \(c+d\mathrm i\ne0\). The new denominator is \(c^2+d^2\).

For real \(a,b,u,v\) and \(z=u+v\mathrm i\), the expression \(az+bz^*\) is \((a+b)u+(a-b)v\mathrm i\).

examples.title: Read the two components
examples.question: For \(z=-4 + 3 \mathrm{i}\), give \(\operatorname{Re}z\) and \(\operatorname{Im}z\).
examples.solution:
The Cartesian form is \(a+b\mathrm i\). The real part is the term without \(\mathrm i\).

The imaginary part is the real coefficient of \(\mathrm i\), so the two values are \(-4\) and \(3\).

examples.title: Add or subtract matching components
examples.question: Calculate \((2 + 5 \mathrm{i})+(-3 + 2 \mathrm{i})\). Give the pair (real part, imaginary part).
examples.solution:
Combine the real parts: \(2+(-3)=-1\).

Do the same for the imaginary parts: \(5+(2)=7\).

The result is \(-1 + 7 \mathrm{i}\).

examples.title: Add or subtract matching components
examples.question: Calculate \((4 - 3 \mathrm{i})-(2 + 4 \mathrm{i})\). Give the pair (real part, imaginary part).
examples.solution:
Combine the real parts: \(4-(2)=2\).

Do the same for the imaginary parts: \(-3-(4)=-7\).

The result is \(2 - 7 \mathrm{i}\).

examples.title: Expand a Cartesian product
examples.question: Multiply \(\left(3 - 2 \mathrm{i}\right)\left(-1 + 4 \mathrm{i}\right)\). Give the pair (real part, imaginary part).
examples.solution:
Use all four terms. The product of the two imaginary terms is \(8\) because \(\mathrm i^2=-1\).

The real part is \((3)(-1)-(-2)(4)=5\).

The cross terms give imaginary part \((3)(4)+(-2)(-1)=14\), so the product is \(5 + 14 \mathrm{i}\).

lessons.title: Complex roots, real polynomials and exact square roots
lessons.summary: Solve quadratics with negative discriminants, use conjugate pairs in real polynomials and find both exact Cartesian square roots.
lessons.objective: Find complete sets of complex roots and explain when conjugation applies.
lessons.before: Recall the quadratic formula, polynomial division and multiplication in Cartesian form.
lessons.method:
1. Use both signs when solving a square equation.
  2. For a real polynomial, remove the monic quadratic formed by the conjugate pair.
  3. For Cartesian square roots, find the two squared components, then pair their signs.
mistakes: Conjugate pairing depends on real coefficients.
A square root and its negative are the two roots of a nonzero complex number.
Taking the square root of a squared sum gives the non-negative sum.
lessons.ideas:
If \(d>0\), then the solutions of \(w^2=-d\) are \(w=\pm\mathrm i\sqrt d\).

If \(p(z)=0\) and the coefficients of \(p\) are real, then \(p(z^*)=p(z)^*=0\). For a non-real root the two roots are distinct.

For roots \(a+b\mathrm i\) and \(a-b\mathrm i\), their monic factor is \((z-a)^2+b^2\).

The known factor accounts for two degrees. Use the remaining degree to check that the final root list is complete.

\(u^2-v^2=A,\quad 2uv=B,\quad u^2+v^2=\sqrt{A^2+B^2}\). Add and subtract to get the two squared magnitudes. Then use the product to couple the signs.

If \(z>0\) is real its roots are real. If \(z<0\) is real its roots are purely imaginary. For zero the only distinct root is zero.

examples.title: Solve a quadratic with no real roots
examples.question: Solve \(z^{2} - 6 z + 13=0\). Enter both pairs (real part, imaginary part).
examples.solution:
The discriminant is \(-16\). A negative discriminant gives two non-real roots.

The equivalent completed form is \((z-(3))^2=-4\). Its two square roots are \(\pm 2\mathrm i\).

Adding \(3\) gives \(3 + 2 \mathrm{i},\quad 3 - 2 \mathrm{i}\).

examples.title: Solve a quadratic with no real roots
examples.question: Solve \(2 z^{2} + 8 z + 26=0\). Enter both pairs (real part, imaginary part).
examples.solution:
The discriminant is \(-144\). A negative discriminant gives two non-real roots.

The equivalent completed form is \((z-(-2))^2=-9\). Its two square roots are \(\pm 3\mathrm i\).

Adding \(-2\) gives \(-2 + 3 \mathrm{i},\quad -2 - 3 \mathrm{i}\).

examples.title: Make a real quadratic factor
examples.question: A real polynomial has root \(1 + 4 \mathrm{i}\). Give its conjugate as the (real part, imaginary part) pair. Then enter a real quadratic equation with those two roots.
examples.solution:
A real polynomial satisfies \(p(z^*)=p(z)^*\), so the conjugate \(1 - 4 \mathrm{i}\) is also a root.

The corresponding factor is \((z-(1))^2+16\), from the product of the conjugate factors.

On expansion this is \(z^{2} - 2 z + 17\).

examples.title: Remove the known conjugate pair
examples.question: The polynomial \(p(z)=z^{3} - z^{2} - 7 z + 15\) has root \(2 + \mathrm{i}\). Give its conjugate as (real part, imaginary part), then give the remaining real root.
examples.solution:
The given root and its conjugate give the real factor \(z^{2} - 4 z + 5\).

Divide the polynomial by that factor. This gives \(z + 3\) with remainder zero.

The real root is \(-3\).

lessons.title: Modulus, argument and Argand geometry
lessons.summary: Find exact distances and directions, choose the correct quadrant and move between Cartesian and modulus–argument descriptions.
lessons.objective: Connect Argand coordinates to modulus and argument and apply the geometry to two points.
lessons.before: Recall Pythagoras, exact trigonometric values and measuring angles in radians.
lessons.method:
1. Find the distance from the origin using Pythagoras.
  2. Locate the point and choose the angle in the requested interval.
  3. Use cosine and sine for the components, or subtract the two points first to find a displacement.
mistakes: Inverse tangent on its own does not identify the correct quadrant.
The length between two points uses the difference of their positions.
lessons.ideas:
\(|a+b\mathrm i|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) and \(|z|^2=zz^*\). The modulus of zero is zero.

For non-zero real component, the reference angle has tangent \(\left|\frac ba\right|\). The quadrant determines how to convert that angle.

Use the interval specified. The common choices are \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\) and \(0\le\theta<2\pi\). On the negative real axis the argument is \(\pi\) in both.

For modulus \(r\) and angle \(\theta\), the point is \((r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\).

The distance is \(|b-a|\); the direction of the movement, when the points differ, is \(\arg(b-a)\).

A non-zero number with argument \(\theta\) has a conjugate whose argument is \(-\theta\) modulo \(2\pi\). Put the result back into the specified interval.

examples.title: Find distance from the origin
examples.question: Find the modulus of \(-7 + 24 \mathrm{i}\).
examples.solution:
The two Cartesian components are \(-7\) and \(24\).

By Pythagoras the modulus is \(\sqrt{(-7)^2+(24)^2}=25\).

examples.title: Choose the argument in the stated interval
examples.question: Find the exact argument of \(- 5 \sqrt{3} + 5 \mathrm{i}\) in radians with \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).
examples.solution:
Use the point \(\left(- 5 \sqrt{3},5\right)\) to fix the direction.

The signs put the point in quadrant II. The acute reference angle is \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). In the stated interval that gives \(\frac{5 \pi}{6}\).

examples.title: Choose the argument in the stated interval
examples.question: Find the exact argument of \(-4 - 4 \mathrm{i}\) in radians with \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).
examples.solution:
Use the point \(\left(-4,-4\right)\) to fix the direction.

The signs put the point in quadrant III. The acute reference angle is \(\frac{\pi}{4}\). In the stated interval that gives \(- \frac{3 \pi}{4}\).

examples.title: Choose the argument in the stated interval
examples.question: Find the exact argument of \(-9\) in radians with \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).
examples.solution:
Use the point \(\left(-9,0\right)\) to fix the direction.

The point lies on an axis. From the positive real axis, the required direction in the stated interval is \(\pi\).

lessons.title: Polar and exponential calculations
lessons.summary: Choose a useful representation, multiply and divide with exact arguments, and find both square roots in polar or exponential form.
lessons.objective: Calculate with non-zero complex numbers in polar and exponential form and interpret the corresponding geometry.
lessons.before: Revise exact trigonometric values, principal arguments and changes of interval.
lessons.method:
1. Represent a non-zero position by its radius and direction.
  2. Multiply or divide the radii and add or subtract the angles.
  3. For square roots, halve two target angles a full turn apart.
mistakes: Angles combine by addition or subtraction.
Reduce the result to the requested angle interval.
Always account for both square-root directions.
lessons.ideas:
\(e^{\mathrm i\theta}=\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta\). Therefore \(re^{\mathrm i\theta}\) and \(r(\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)\) describe the same point.

\((re^{\mathrm i\alpha})(se^{\mathrm i\beta})=rse^{\mathrm i(\alpha+\beta)}\). Reduce the result to the interval requested.

\(\frac{re^{\mathrm i\alpha}}{se^{\mathrm i\beta}}=\frac rs e^{\mathrm i(\alpha-\beta)}\), where \(s>0\).

The rotation is about the origin. For a divisor of modulus r, the new distance is the old distance multiplied by its reciprocal.

For a non-zero target \(re^{\mathrm i\theta}\), take modulus \(\sqrt r\) and directions \(\frac{\theta}{2}\) and \(\frac{\theta}{2}+\pi\). Normalise each separately.

On the negative real axis use the included argument pi if the principal interval is requested. Its two square-root rays are the positive and negative imaginary axes.

examples.title: Switch from Cartesian to polar form
examples.question: Give the two parameters (modulus, argument in radians) of \(-5 + 5 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{i}\) in polar form. Use \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).
examples.solution:
Pythagoras gives the radius \(10\) from the components \(-5\) and \(5 \sqrt{3}\).

The direction of the point from the origin gives angle \(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\) in the required interval.

In polar form this is \(10\left(\cos\left(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)+\mathrm i\sin\left(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)\right)\).

examples.title: Switch from Cartesian to exponential form
examples.question: Give the two parameters (modulus, argument in radians) of \(4 \sqrt{2} - 4 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{i}\) in exponential form. Use \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).
examples.solution:
Pythagoras gives the radius \(8\) from the components \(4 \sqrt{2}\) and \(- 4 \sqrt{2}\).

The direction of the point from the origin gives angle \(- \frac{\pi}{4}\) in the required interval.

In exponential form this is \(8e^{\mathrm i\left(- \frac{\pi}{4}\right)}\).

examples.title: Find the polar product
examples.question: Take \(u=2e^{\mathrm i\left(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)}\) and \(v=3e^{\mathrm i\left(\frac{3 \pi}{4}\right)}\). Give \(uv\) as the pair (modulus, argument in radians), with \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).
examples.solution:
Multiply the moduli to obtain \(6\).

Add the direction angles to obtain \(\frac{17 \pi}{12}\) before changing intervals.

Reduce by whole turns if needed. The requested angle is \(- \frac{7 \pi}{12}\), giving \(6e^{\mathrm i\left(- \frac{7 \pi}{12}\right)}\).

examples.title: Find the polar quotient
examples.question: Take \(u=12e^{\mathrm i\left(- \frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)}\) and \(v=4e^{\mathrm i\left(\frac{3 \pi}{4}\right)}\). Give \(\frac uv\) as the pair (modulus, argument in radians), with \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).
examples.solution:
Divide the moduli to obtain \(3\).

Subtract the direction angles to obtain \(- \frac{17 \pi}{12}\) before changing intervals.

Reduce by whole turns if needed. The requested angle is \(\frac{7 \pi}{12}\), giving \(3e^{\mathrm i\left(\frac{7 \pi}{12}\right)}\).

lessons.title: Argand loci and regions
lessons.summary: Turn modulus and argument conditions into circles, bisectors and rays, and identify shared regions with the correct boundaries.
lessons.objective: Sketch simple Argand circles, bisectors, rays and combined regions from equations and inequalities.
lessons.before: Recall coordinates, the distance formula and angles measured from the positive real direction.
lessons.method:
1. Interpret each modulus or argument as a condition on a displacement.
  2. Mark a fixed point, circle, bisector or ray, then choose the included boundaries.
  3. For simultaneous conditions keep the intersection of the allowed sets.
mistakes: A strict distance inequality excludes its boundary.
Equal distances give a perpendicular bisector.
The vertex of an argument ray is excluded.
lessons.ideas:
\(|z-a|=r\) is the circle centred at \(a\) with radius \(r>0\). The inequality \(|z-a|<r\) keeps the interior and \(|z-a|>r\) keeps the exterior.

\(|z-a|=|z-b|\) gives a line. Squaring both non-negative distances cancels the quadratic terms in the two variables.

\(\arg(z-a)=\alpha\) means \(z=a+t(\cos\alpha+\mathrm i\sin\alpha)\) for \(t>0\).

Use a solid boundary for equality allowed and dashed for equality excluded. When an argument is involved, mark an open circle at any excluded endpoint.

Write \((x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2\) for centre \((h,k)\). A positive remaining square gives two intersection positions.

A point at the centre satisfies every positive-radius disc constraint. It fails a direction constraint based at that centre.

examples.title: Read a circle and its boundary
examples.question: For \(|z-\left(1 - 2 \mathrm{i}\right)|<3\), give the Cartesian equation of the circle centred at the fixed point. Then select the intended region.
examples.solution:
The fixed point is \(1 - 2 \mathrm{i}\). Interpret the modulus as distance from \(\left(1,-2\right)\).

Setting the distance equal to \(3\) gives the boundary \(\left(x - 1\right)^{2} + \left(y + 2\right)^{2}=9\).

Inside the circle, with the boundary excluded.

examples.title: Read a circle and its boundary
examples.question: For \(|z-\left(-2 + \mathrm{i}\right)|\le4\), give the Cartesian equation of the circle centred at the fixed point. Then select the intended region.
examples.solution:
The fixed point is \(-2 + \mathrm{i}\). Interpret the modulus as distance from \(\left(-2,1\right)\).

Setting the distance equal to \(4\) gives the boundary \(\left(x + 2\right)^{2} + \left(y - 1\right)^{2}=16\).

Inside the circle and on its boundary.

examples.title: Find the perpendicular bisector
examples.question: Let \(a=1 + 2 \mathrm{i}\) and \(b=5 + 4 \mathrm{i}\). Give the midpoint as (real part, imaginary part), then enter the Cartesian equation of \(|z-a|=|z-b|\).
examples.solution:
The two moduli are non-negative distances. Equal distances define the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the two fixed points.

The midpoint is \(3 + 3 \mathrm{i}\). After squaring the distances, the two squared variable terms cancel.

The resulting line is \(2 x + y - 9=0\).

examples.title: Identify a ray and its endpoint
examples.question: For \(\arg\!\left(z-\left(2 - \mathrm{i}\right)\right)=\frac{\pi}{4}\), give the endpoint coordinates and choose the point that belongs to the locus.
examples.solution:
The argument measures the direction of the displacement from \(2 - \mathrm{i}\), so the endpoint is \(\left(2,-1\right)\).

Moving from the endpoint by \(1 + \mathrm{i}\) follows the required ray and reaches \(3\).

The endpoint is excluded because the zero displacement has no argument.

questions.title: Add or subtract matching components
questions.prompt_html: Calculate \((8 + 3 \mathrm{i})-(2 - 4 \mathrm{i})\). Give the pair (real part, imaginary part).
questions.solution_html:
Combine the real parts: \(8-(2)=6\).

Do the same for the imaginary parts: \(3-(-4)=7\).

The result is \(6 + 7 \mathrm{i}\).
questions.hint_html: Keep the brackets when subtracting.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the correct pair (real part, imaginary part).

questions.title: Add or subtract matching components
questions.prompt_html: Calculate \((5 - 6 \mathrm{i})-(-1 + 2 \mathrm{i})\). Give the pair (real part, imaginary part).
questions.solution_html:
Combine the real parts: \(5-(-1)=6\).

Do the same for the imaginary parts: \(-6-(2)=-8\).

The result is \(6 - 8 \mathrm{i}\).
questions.hint_html: Keep the brackets when subtracting.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the correct pair (real part, imaginary part).

questions.title: Expand a Cartesian product
questions.prompt_html: Multiply \(\left(2 - 3 \mathrm{i}\right)\left(3 + 5 \mathrm{i}\right)\). Give the pair (real part, imaginary part).
questions.solution_html:
Use all four terms. The product of the two imaginary terms is \(15\) because \(\mathrm i^2=-1\).

The real part is \((2)(3)-(-3)(5)=21\).

The cross terms give imaginary part \((2)(5)+(-3)(3)=1\), so the product is \(21 + \mathrm{i}\).
questions.hint_html: The term involving i squared belongs to the real part.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the correct pair (real part, imaginary part).

questions.title: Expand a Cartesian product
questions.prompt_html: Multiply \(\left(-4 + \mathrm{i}\right)\left(2 - 3 \mathrm{i}\right)\). Give the pair (real part, imaginary part).
questions.solution_html:
Use all four terms. The product of the two imaginary terms is \(3\) because \(\mathrm i^2=-1\).

The real part is \((-4)(2)-(1)(-3)=-5\).

The cross terms give imaginary part \((-4)(-3)+(1)(2)=14\), so the product is \(-5 + 14 \mathrm{i}\).
questions.hint_html: The term involving i squared belongs to the real part.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the correct pair (real part, imaginary part).

questions.title: Reflect in the real axis
questions.prompt_html: For \(z=3 - 5 \mathrm{i}\), give \(z^*\) as (real part, imaginary part), then calculate \(zz^*\).
questions.solution_html:
Keep the real component and change the sign of the imaginary component. This gives \(z^*=3 + 5 \mathrm{i}\).

The cross terms cancel in the product, leaving \((a+b\mathrm i)(a-b\mathrm i)=a^2+b^2\).

Here the product is \(34\).
questions.hint_html: Conjugation reverses only the imaginary part.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the correct pair (real part, imaginary part).
Give the correct real product.

questions.title: Reflect in the real axis
questions.prompt_html: For \(z=-5 + 2 \mathrm{i}\), give \(z^*\) as (real part, imaginary part), then calculate \(zz^*\).
questions.solution_html:
Keep the real component and change the sign of the imaginary component. This gives \(z^*=-5 - 2 \mathrm{i}\).

The cross terms cancel in the product, leaving \((a+b\mathrm i)(a-b\mathrm i)=a^2+b^2\).

Here the product is \(29\).
questions.hint_html: Conjugation reverses only the imaginary part.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the correct pair (real part, imaginary part).
Give the correct real product.

questions.title: Make the denominator real
questions.prompt_html: Express \(\frac{2 + 7 \mathrm{i}}{4 + 3 \mathrm{i}}\) as a (real part, imaginary part) pair.
questions.solution_html:
Multiply numerator and denominator by \(4 - 3 \mathrm{i}\). This keeps the ratio unchanged.

The denominator becomes \(25\) and the numerator becomes \(29 + 22 \mathrm{i}\).

Divide both components by \(25\) to obtain \(\frac{29}{25} + \frac{22 \mathrm{i}}{25}\).
questions.hint_html: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the original denominator.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the correct pair (real part, imaginary part).

questions.title: Make the denominator real
questions.prompt_html: Express \(\frac{11 - 3 \mathrm{i}}{2 - 5 \mathrm{i}}\) as a (real part, imaginary part) pair.
questions.solution_html:
Multiply numerator and denominator by \(2 + 5 \mathrm{i}\). This keeps the ratio unchanged.

The denominator becomes \(29\) and the numerator becomes \(37 + 49 \mathrm{i}\).

Divide both components by \(29\) to obtain \(\frac{37}{29} + \frac{49 \mathrm{i}}{29}\).
questions.hint_html: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the original denominator.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the correct pair (real part, imaginary part).

questions.title: Link two Cartesian calculations
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(a=2 - 5 \mathrm{i}\), \(b=3 + \mathrm{i}\) and \(q=4 - 2 \mathrm{i}\). Work in Cartesian form.

  1. Find \(ab\). [2]

  2. Find \(a-q\). [1]

  3. Solve \(bw+q=a\) for \(w\). Show how the denominator becomes real. [3]
questions.solution_html:
1. Use all four terms. The product of the two imaginary terms is \(5\) because \(\mathrm i^2=-1\).

    The real part is \((2)(3)-(-5)(1)=11\).

    The cross terms give imaginary part \((2)(1)+(-5)(3)=-13\), so the product is \(11 - 13 \mathrm{i}\).

  2. Combine the real parts: \(2-(4)=-2\).

    Do the same for the imaginary parts: \(-5-(-2)=-3\).

    The result is \(-2 - 3 \mathrm{i}\).

  3. Rearrange before dividing by the non-zero number b.

    Multiply numerator and denominator by \(3 - \mathrm{i}\). This keeps the ratio unchanged.

    The denominator becomes \(10\) and the numerator becomes \(-9 - 7 \mathrm{i}\).

    Divide both components by \(10\) to obtain \(- \frac{9}{10} - \frac{7 \mathrm{i}}{10}\).
questions.hint_html: The difference in part (b) is the numerator needed in part (c).

marking_criteria.description_html: Expand all four products with the correct value of i squared.
Obtain both Cartesian components.
Give the correct real and imaginary components.
Rearrange to a difference divided by b.
Multiply by the conjugate of b above and below.
Give the exact Cartesian number.

questions.title: Recover a point, then move it to the real axis
questions.prompt_html:
A point represents \(z=u+v\mathrm i\), where \(u,v\) are real, and \((3-2\mathrm i)z+(1+4\mathrm i)=13+9\mathrm i\).

  1. Expand the product and express its real and imaginary parts in terms of u and v. [2]

  2. Find \(z\), showing two real equations. [3]

  3. Find the real \(\lambda\) for which \(z+\lambda(1-2\mathrm i)\) is real. Give the resulting real value. [2]
questions.answer_html:
1. Real part \(3u+2v\), imaginary part \(3v-2u\).

  2. \(2 + 3 \mathrm{i}\).

  3. \(\lambda=\frac32\) and the real value \(\frac{7}{2}\).
questions.solution_html:
1. Use \(-2\mathrm i\cdot v\mathrm i=2v\), then collect \(3u+2v\) and \(3v-2u\).

  2. Subtract \(1 + 4 \mathrm{i}\) first. Matching components gives \(3u+2v=12\) and \(3v-2u=5\).

    Three times the first equation minus twice the second gives \(13u=26\). Hence \(u=2\) and \(v=3\).

  3. Set the imaginary component \(3-2\lambda\) to zero. This gives \(\lambda=\frac32\).

    The real part becomes \(2+\frac32=\frac72\).
questions.hint_html: Subtract the fixed term first, then compare coefficients of the two components.

marking_criteria.description_html: Expand all four products using i squared equals minus one.
Obtain both components.
Obtain the simultaneous real equations.
Eliminate either variable.
Give both components of z.
Set the imaginary component to zero.
Give the correct multiplier and resulting real value.

questions.title: A hidden conjugate equation
questions.prompt_html:
A complex number \(z\) satisfies \(3z+z^*=8 - 10 \mathrm{i}\).

  1. Find \(z\). [3]

  2. Find \(zz^*\) and give the geometric relationship between \(z\) and \(z^*\) in the Argand plane. [2]

  3. Solve \((z^*+1)u=z\) for \(u\). [3]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(2 - 5 \mathrm{i}\).

  2. \(zz^*=29\). The two points are reflections in the real axis.

  3. \(- \frac{19}{34} - \frac{25 \mathrm{i}}{34}\).
questions.solution_html:
1. The left side is \((a+b)u+(a-b)v\mathrm i\) for weights \(a=3,b=1\).

    Equate the real terms and imaginary coefficients: \(4u=8\) and \(2v=-10\).

    Therefore \(z=2 - 5 \mathrm{i}\).

  2. Keep the real component and change the sign of the imaginary component. This gives \(z^*=2 + 5 \mathrm{i}\).

    The cross terms cancel in the product, leaving \((a+b\mathrm i)(a-b\mathrm i)=a^2+b^2\).

    Here the product is \(29\).

    The Cartesian vertical coordinate changes sign.

  3. Multiply numerator and denominator by \(3 - 5 \mathrm{i}\). This keeps the ratio unchanged.

    The denominator becomes \(34\) and the numerator becomes \(-19 - 25 \mathrm{i}\).

    Divide both components by \(34\) to obtain \(- \frac{19}{34} - \frac{25 \mathrm{i}}{34}\).
questions.hint_html: The imaginary part of the conjugate has the opposite sign to the imaginary part of z.

marking_criteria.description_html: Write the two equations using real and imaginary coefficients.

Obtain the correct imaginary part.
Obtain the real product.

questions.title: Solve a quadratic with no real roots
questions.prompt_html: Solve \(z^{2} - 4 z + 29=0\). Enter both pairs (real part, imaginary part).

fields.label: All root pairs (real part, imaginary part)

questions.solution_html:
The discriminant is \(-100\). A negative discriminant gives two non-real roots.

The equivalent completed form is \((z-(2))^2=-25\). Its two square roots are \(\pm 5\mathrm i\).

Adding \(2\) gives \(2 + 5 \mathrm{i},\quad 2 - 5 \mathrm{i}\).
questions.hint_html: After completing the square or using the formula, take both square roots of the negative number.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the correct all root pairs (real part, imaginary part).

questions.title: Solve a quadratic with no real roots
questions.prompt_html: Solve \(z^{2} + 6 z + 25=0\). Enter both pairs (real part, imaginary part).

fields.label: All root pairs (real part, imaginary part)

questions.title: Use the geometry of both square roots
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(z=-8 - 8 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{i}\).

  1. Express \(z\) in exponential form with its argument in \((-\pi,\pi]\). [2]

  2. Find both square roots in exponential form with angles in \([0,2\pi)\). [3]

  3. Give the root with positive real part in exact Cartesian form and state the angle between the two root rays. [3]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(16e^{\mathrm i\left(- \frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)}\).

  2. \(4e^{\mathrm i\left(\frac{5 \pi}{3}\right)}\) and \(4e^{\mathrm i\left(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)}\).

  3. \(2 - 2 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{i}\) and \(\pi\) radians.
questions.solution_html:
1. Pythagoras gives the radius \(16\) from the components \(-8\) and \(- 8 \sqrt{3}\).

    The direction of the point from the origin gives angle \(- \frac{2 \pi}{3}\) in the required interval.

    In exponential form this is \(16e^{\mathrm i\left(- \frac{2 \pi}{3}\right)}\).

  2. Squaring doubles the direction and squares the modulus. Each root has modulus \(4\).

    Doubling angles is modulo \(2\pi\), so first use \(- \frac{2 \pi}{3}\) and \(\frac{4 \pi}{3}\) as target directions.

    Halve each angle and reduce to the stated interval. The two arguments are \(\frac{5 \pi}{3}\) and \(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\).

    The roots are opposite points on the Argand diagram.

  3. The positive-real root has direction \(\frac{5 \pi}{3}\) in the specified interval.

    Project the radius onto the axes to obtain \(2 - 2 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{i}\). The second root is the negative, so the two rays differ by \(\pi\).
questions.hint_html: Square roots have equal moduli. The directions differ by half a turn.

    The squared distance is \(5t^2\). Therefore \(t=\pm1\), which gives \(\left(1,4\right),\quad \left(3,0\right)\).
